    #112195. Louisa Jacobson’s Stylist on 10 Things That Inspire Her Red Carpet Looks

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1410 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Harpersbazaar ↗ Open Full Page

    Louisa Jacobson’s Stylist on 10 Things That Inspire Her Red Carpet Looks

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In fashion, anything from niche archival research to a favorite film to an outfit you saw on your morning commute can make for inspiration.
    • In a recent development, method dressing has become the road most traveled for Hollywood A-listers and their stylists.
    • According to recent reports, “One thing that we are always aware of is not being the character she plays on TV, because she is more than that,” Jacobson’s stylist Edward Bowleg III told Harper’s Bazaar over Zoom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In fashion, anything from niche archival research to a favorite film to an outfit you saw on your morning commute can make for inspiration. In our upcoming series 10 Things, we ask industry professionals and tastemakers to divulge the (you guessed it) 10 things that had the most impact on their aesthetic choices.

    In a recent development, method dressing has become the road most traveled for Hollywood A-listers and their stylists. We’ve seen Zendaya and Law Roach turn out goddess-like dresses in homage to the actress’s role of Athena in The Odyssey, while the cast of the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has been channeling their outlandish onscreen personas into equally over-the-top red carpet looks. But even though period pieces present a prime opportunity for imitation, The Gilded Age star Louisa Jacobson, who plays Marian Brook in the Julian Fellowes series, indicates she’d rather dress like herself.

    According to recent reports, “One thing that we are always aware of is not being the character she plays on TV, because she is more than that,” Jacobson’s stylist Edward Bowleg III told Harper’s Bazaar over Zoom. “She is a fully fleshed-out human being. She is Louisa and she is not Marian. That is an crucial distinction.”.

    According to recent reports, bowleg started working with the actress in 2022 after a mutual friend introduced them right around the time that The Gilded Age was set to premiere. The editorial stylist, who has worked for countless publications and brands like Hermès, Valentino, and Marc Jacobs, recalls his first official project with Jacobson: the 2022 Vanity Fair Oscars party, to which she wore an ivory off-the-shoulder Khaite gown with a Jeffrey Levinson clutch.

    Recent findings suggest that much has changed in the four years since that evening. “When she cut her hair short, that was the moment where a lot shifted,” noted Bowleg. “It was a new her.” With the fresh haircut came a slew of delightfully unexpected red carpet moments, spanning a handful of tailored suits (and a cummerbund!) from Haider Ackermann’s Tom Ford, Conner Ives, and Calvin Klein Collection to a Dilara Findikoglu minidress with an armored bodice made from safety pins, metal accents, and a tattered chiffon train.

    Industry observers note that jacobson’s fashion evolution paralleled her own self-actualization. “Exploring sexual identity and being more free with that led to having more fun with experimental fashion and being unapologetic about what she likes and who she is,” said Bowleg. And it demonstrates: She’s been on a winning style streak recently.

    Coming off Jacobson’s recent Gilded Age press tour, which saw looks from Haider Ackermann’s Tom Ford, Ashlyn, Commission, and Mel Usine, Bowleg sat down with Bazaar to decode 10 influences that shaped his fashion choices, from Saint Laurent’s le smoking to an Azzedine Alaïa collection that lives rent-free in his head.

    According to recent reports, “We love tailoring, we love a suit. I could have her in a suit every day of the week. She went to her first Tom Ford show in March. When she told me she was invited, I was like ‘Oh my god, that is so cool,’ because I am a major fan. The 1996 Gucci show is burned into my brain. That is when my interest in fashion really began, so for me in a weird way it was almost like a full circle moment.

    Industry observers note that “I think with creative director Haider Ackermann’s tailoring in particular, the cut is so exquisite. When we have fittings with them, the only thing we are adjusting is the length of the trousers. There is also a confidence that she has when she puts them on. It’s very commanding. Then you mix that in with all of the elements—there is always a really sexy shoe that goes along with it.”.

    “An image that could have been on the moodboard would be Helmut Newton’s photos of Saint Laurent’s Le Smoking with the women on the street in Paris. There is one image with a naked woman wearing just heels, standing with another woman in Le Smoking. That is very much the kind of vibe we are going for: mixing something sexy and feminine with tailoring, which is inherently masculine.”.

    In a recent development, “She went to the Met Gala this year with Dilara [Findikoglu]. When I had the conversation with Dilara and her team, the idea of armor came up. She had been to the Met ahead of our conversation, and she sent me all of these pictures that she had taken in the Medieval section where they have the helmets and the chain mail and the body armor. Those were just things that she loved and that became a big inspiration for the look.”.

    Sources indicate that “For Louisa’s first Met Gala in 2022 (the red carpet theme was ‘Gilded Glamour, White Tie’) there was a John Singer Sargent painting of a woman in a black dress. The image helped direct our choice of look”—a futuristic gown with a gold trompe l'œil skeleton molded in leather and hand-painted in gold leaf from the Schiaparelli Spring/Summer 2022 Haute Couture collection by Daniel Roseberry.

    It has been revealed that “I love Azzedine Alaïa. Specifically the 1986 show—the one with all of the bandage dressing with the cut-outs on the sides and the infamous denim and leather zip that goes all across the body. I believe Grace Jones walked. Even with the McQueen that she just wore, in a way it’s that sort of vibe—the bomber jacket but with the little skirt. It’s that kind of energy: A strong, powerful woman.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “There has been quite a bit of leather. The McQueen that she just wore, the Khaite full leather suit that she wore to the Vanity Fair Oscars party. She put it on, and it was like ‘This is fab.’ We were wondering if it was right for Vanity Fair and whether she would be the only one in a suit. I told Louisa that Zendaya had worn a suit the year before and I also was kind of like, ‘Fuck it, you look hot, this is great.’ Then there were two more leather Louis Vuitton looks that she wore. One was to the Vanity Fair Oscars party in 2024. And then before that, she wore a Vuitton look to the SAG Awards and the whole bodice was sculpted in leather, as well.”.

    It has been revealed that “Hedi Slimane is a massive inspiration of mine. Again, it’s a lot of tailoring, it’s leather, it’s a great silhouette. It’s the aesthetic overall, but in particular, it was the fall/winter 2006 collection that he did. There were things that were skinny and then there were things that were a bit more loose in terms of the trousers. There was a softness to the hardness of it all. It was still very edgy and a bit rock ‘n’ roll, but there was a soft glamour to it. That is something that I like with Louisa, even when it comes to the jewelry.”.

    Sources indicate that “I am really curious to see what Pieter Mulier will do with Versace and Atelier Versace is in January. [I should also say that] I am obsessed with Donatella Versace. When I started looking at all things [high] fashion, Donatella was another designer that I loved. That glamour and excess and sexiness—she is unapologetically who she is.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “With music and ‘90s hip-hop, you look at the bling, the diamonds, and things like that. I love a great jewelry moment, so accessorizing Louisa’s looks with the right jewelry is always key part to me. I love diamonds. When she recently went to a Tiffany & Co. event [in Ashlyn], we initially had our brooch up on the lapel where you would traditionally see it. Then she was like, ‘It doesn’t feel right.’ So I moved it down to the peplum of the jacket. It was a substantial, big yellow diamond, which I was obsessed with. I just loved how much it sparkled and shined.”.

    According to recent reports, “Helmut Lang is also a substantial inspiration. There is a Spring 1998 men's collection and a Spring 1999 collection that I think about a lot in terms of silhouette and things that still resonate today. It all comes from having researched some of those collections in the past, so they tend to be recurring elements in the work.”.

    #112180. Designers Say This ’70s-Inspired Design Trend Is Making a Glamorous Comeback

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (536 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    Designers Say This ’70s-Inspired Design Trend Is Making a Glamorous Comeback

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (536 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Whether it’s in our personal style, architectural splendor, or cultural ties, great design mirrors the world around us.
    • Once dismissed as a tacky, ’70s-era trend (not unlike wood paneling), mirrored surfaces are making a comeback.
    • “I love mirrored surfaces in interiors because they can be so transformative & work in all styles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We all know design is reflective. Whether it’s in our personal style, architectural splendor, or cultural ties, great design mirrors the world around us. Now, it’s time for it to mirror itself.

    Once dismissed as a tacky, ’70s-era trend (not unlike wood paneling), mirrored surfaces are making a comeback. But don’t worry—today’s mirror craze moves past the floor-to-ceiling panels of the past, opting instead for accents that add light, depth, and dimension.

    “I love mirrored surfaces in interiors because they can be so transformative & work in all styles. They can add glitz and glamour, especially when you add beveled details,” claims Bridget Tiek of TIEK BYDAY. “I love to see mirrors as a backbar, behind shelves, on doors, ceilings and on walls. Basically everywhere!”.

    According to recent reports, bolder than traditional ready-to-hang mirrors, mirrored surfaces are often hard to place tastefully. Here’s how designers have brought the striking detail into interiors.

    Queer Eye for the Straight Guy star Carson Kressley’s Murray Hill apartment is full of personality, and his sunken living room has several glittering surfaces. The designer embraces mirrored shine as a bold accent, as seen in this disco-ball-tiled end table.

    Use It for a Bold Bar Backsplash.

    Recent findings suggest that designer Alexander D. Wilson brought a mirrored backsplash into this Upper East Side apartment to elevate the elegant yet fun palette while creating the illusion of a larger space. NYC apartments often feel like a shoebox. With this classic design trick, they don’t have to look like it.

    Industry observers note that interior designer Sarah Vaile brought Manhattan to the Windy City in this punchy coastal home. After coating the walls in Farrow & Ball’s Borrowed Light for a classic Nancy Meyers-esque aesthetic, she framed a nearly ceiling-high mirror in crisp white molding, transforming the panel into a bold decorative piece that amplifies space and cosmopolitan chic.

    Incorporate as a Tasteful Touch.

    Bold enough to make a fierce statement in even the smallest piece, interior designer Amy Courtney brought industrial flair to her New York City home with a silvery domed lamp to complement the bold hues of her living room’s palette.

    While the glassy, expansive nature of mirrored panels certainly has its charms, if you’re hoping to bring both glossy and textured flair to your design, mirrored tiles are the perfect solution. Designer Shannon Ggem used mirrored tiles in this moody bar design to bring more light to the room without sacrificing the deep-hued palette.

    While most rely on millwork to bring style to the walls, designer Michelle Prentice opted for mirror panels on the closet doors of this South Carolina bedroom. Not only do they add depth to the design, but they bring a boutique feel while adding to the visual palette and playing off the centered vanity mirror to unify the wall treatments.

    In a recent development, as stainless steel fades from an industry standard to a passing fad, designers are getting creative when it comes to finding chic alternatives. In this monochrome green butler’s pantry, designer Bridget Tiek brought in a glassy paneled door to elevate the appliance design, taking the invisible kitchen trend to new heights.

    #112168. Tech Report: Fashion Has Moved Beyond the Runway and Into the Director’s Chair

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (951 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elle ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Fashion Has Moved Beyond the Runway and Into the Director’s Chair

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ahead of Matthieu Blazy’s first Chanel Métiers d’art show, Michel Gondry introduced the collection’s world through a surreal short starring Margaret Qualley and A$AP Rocky.
    • Industry observers note that when guests, including Rocky and Qualley, arrived at the show, the story continued where the film had left off.
    • It has been revealed that fashion’s love affair with the silver screen stretches across decades.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ahead of Matthieu Blazy’s first Chanel Métiers d’art show, Michel Gondry introduced the collection’s world through a surreal short starring Margaret Qualley and A$AP Rocky. Released as a prelude to the runway, the film follows the couple as they drift through Upcoming York along parallel paths before finding each other again on a downtown sidewalk, where Rocky proposes moments before they disappear into the subway station together.

    Industry observers note that when guests, including Rocky and Qualley, arrived at the show, the story continued where the film had left off. Bhavitha Mandava emerged in silk “jeans,” followed later by Mona Tougaard, Anok Yai, and Alex Consani, each embodying a different New York archetype, from the sharply tailored power executive to the impeccably dressed society woman. As they moved through the decommissioned station at Bowery and Kenmare Street in Blazy’s reimagined tweeds, the everyday commute took on a cinematic quality. “Designers are directors themselves, except we’re all their actors,” states Jane Rosenthal, an Academy Award-nominated producer, co-founder of the Tribeca Festival, and co-chair of the board of Tribeca Enterprises. “When they create characters this vivid, they’re creating not just a dress, but a feeling people want to inhabit.”.

    It has been revealed that fashion’s love affair with the silver screen stretches across decades. Coco Chanel designed costumes for two Jean Renoir films; Hubert de Givenchy created Audrey Hepburn’s black sheath dress for Breakfast at Tiffany’s. Today, the relationship runs in both directions. Julian Klausner’s spring/summer 2027 collection for Dries Van Noten borrowed the language of cinema through imagined movie posters splashed on slips and party skirts, while the Angelina Jolie-starring Couture turned its attention to the women behind the seams.

    Sources indicate that and as film culture enjoys a renaissance of its own, fashion is deepening its relationship with the medium. Letterboxd has turned cinephilia into a social, gamified experience, while celebrities now revel in the chance to highlight their most obscure Criterion Collection favorites. Fashion, ever attuned to shifts in culture, has followed suit, moving beyond the familiar fields of costume design and cinematic campaigns to support and sometimes produce filmmaking itself.

    In a recent development, since 2015, Through Her Lens: The Tribeca Chanel Women’s Filmmaker Program, co-founded by Rosenthal, has paired mentorship with financial support for emerging female and nonbinary filmmakers. This year’s program brought together mentors such as Celine Song and Gina Prince-Bythewood, who worked directly with participants.

    Rosenthal points out that the number of female-directed films has, unfortunately, dipped in recent years. After over a decade of the program, “What we’re finding is that the community is really intentional,” she says. “Our advisory board wants to be here. They come back year after year. They want to be part of it, because they want to help support the next generation.” Miu Miu’s Women’s Tales, established by Miuccia Prada in 2011, has similarly become a platform for female filmmakers—including Ava DuVernay, Claire Denis, and Mona Fastvold—to tell original stories. Those initiatives were early signs of a broader shift.

    Sources indicate that in September, Dior revealed a two-year creative partnership with A24, the studio behind auteur-driven hits like Marty Supreme and Everything Everywhere All at Once, spanning film, theater, and live events at the Cherry Lane Theatre in Manhattan’s West Village. The collaboration was introduced online with a tongue-in-cheek short directed by Aidan Zamiri, in which Sabrina Carpenter, Josh O’Connor, and Drew Starkey auditioned to play Dior creative director Jonathan Anderson. (The announcement kicked off with a companion teaser, featuring Carpenter dressed as Anderson himself, complete with his now instantly recognizable formula of a plaid shirt, jeans, and Salomons.).

    In a recent development, under its former creative director Anthony Vaccarello, Saint Laurent launched Saint Laurent Productions in 2023, backing acclaimed films including Pedro Almodóvar’s Strange Way of Life and Jacques Audiard’s Oscar-winning melodrama Emilia Pérez. And Rolex has also invested in cinema’s future, supporting the Student Academy Awards, which platform emerging filmmakers, partnering with festivals like the New York Film Festival and the Sundance Institute as an official partner and exclusive timepiece, and serving as a founding supporter of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures.

    Industry observers note that tara Maria Gonzalez, a fashion writer and author of the Substack newsletter Cult Classic, notes that film allows brands room to build worlds rather than simply present collections or have their designs live in the endless scroll of social media. “People are growing tired of seeing the same trends,” she explains. “It’s like, ‘Well, why do I need to buy that if everybody else has it?’ When designers align themselves with directors, that adds a level of depth that can also connect to a wider audience.”.

    Industry observers note that look no further than Balenciaga, which enlisted Past Lives and Materialists director Song to helm the short film A Upcoming York Minute. Song built a character study around Sarah Pidgeon, using Pierpaolo Piccioli’s designs as a narrative thread rather than the main attraction. It leaves the viewer to focus on a mood before a product, an inversion of what fashion advertising has traditionally asked us to do. “Brands are [showing] that fashion isn’t just for people who self-identify as ‘fashion people,’” Gonzalez notes. “Fashion has the mass appeal that can speak to anybody who’s interested in storytelling. And one of the most accessible forms of storytellingis film.”.

    Like Gondry’s lovers disappearing into the subway station, the most memorable fashion stories don’t end when the collection arrives on the runway or on the shop floor. They only become more interesting out on the streets, where clothes become characters and the city becomes the set.

    A version of this story appears in the December 2026/January 2027 matter of ELLE.
